utterances.text: No. Not buildings. There are some 30 metres of open space to the command post which is somewhat higher up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, just help me understand it, and we'll get the map out. What's 30 metres away? The command post is 30 metres away from where your living quarters were or from where you were stationed?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: The command post was 30 metres removed from the place where they were looking at the panorama, and our quarters were some 20 metres from the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, and you say that you purportedly saw Mr. Beara on the day of the NATO bombing, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's that same day that you went to see your in laws, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, in the evening, the arrangements at the IKM were completed, and the entire rear was moved from IKM to Bratunac. That was in the morning. And in the evening hours, around 11.00 or 12.00 p.m., we moved to Bratunac from the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I got that and I got the quartermaster part. What I don't understand is this, sir: Where was NATO bombing on that day? Where were they bombing?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: The positions of the Serbian forces in the surroundings of Srebrenica, two times. One position was a rather close, to the command post, some 200 or 300 metres away, and the other position was closer to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So one position was closer to the command post where you were at, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if they are bombing that day, sir, I find it incredible that you would then get up and leave your fellow troops and then go visit your in-laws in some other place for four or five days. You didn't stick around to see if the bombing would continue the next day or the next evening or the next three or four days given specifically because some of the bombing was very close to your very own command post? Is that really true, Mr. Momcilovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on that day, the Srebrenica operation was completed, so the Serbian forces had entered Srebrenica and the IKM was closed down and we moved to Bratunac. There were no more operations conducted from that position. That's why we moved from the IKM to Bratunac because the operation was completed on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, who informed you sir that NATO wouldn't keep bombing on the 12th or 13th or 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No one informed us. But the IKM was closed down. The command and General Krstic and communications, they were all moved, and we received instructions to move the entire rear of the Bratunac Brigade. And after that nobody stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this: Those four or five days that you took to see your family and your in laws, what time was that in?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I left on the 12th, after packing the equipment that was removed from the IKM to the storage facilities and I went to see my children and Sergeant Cvijetinovic did the packing and there was enough time for me to be away for some three or four days. My children were still little at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I have children as well. All I want to know is the name of the town. What town did you go to?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Osamsko which is some ten kilometres from Bratunac on the banks of the Drina. My father-in-law has a house there and that's where they were also.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to clarify this. Did the NATO bombing occur before or after you supposedly or purportedly met Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: There were two bombings, so I think that in between they may have been up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What time --

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know for sure. I'm not certain when it was. But it was on that day. The two bombings took place on the same day and that was all. There was no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Beara come there by a vehicle, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they arrived, nor when they left, because the vehicles wouldn't enter the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, what he was wearing at the time purportedly?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was he wearing civilian clothes, military clothes, the type of military clothes, if you so recall?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember if he wore anything on his head, like a hat or a cap?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you sit here can you describe what he looked like as you recall him on that purported day in between the bombings between NATO when he came?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying to you that Mr. Beara and Mr. Popovic were with Mr. Deronjic, and I remember Mr. Deronjic, whom I had known, and the other two I hadn't known before. I remember that Mr. Deronjic was somewhat taller and had grey hair as compared to Mr. Popovic, but you know people change. I wouldn't know myself now, because at the time I weighed 85 kilos, now I weigh 110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just see in the record at line 14, page 51, there is a reference to Mr. Deronjic as compared to Mr. Popovic, and I'm not sure that's responsive to the question, or an accurate reflection of the answer that the witness gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, those are two things that you raise basically. The first one I would tend to agree with you. As regards the second, on what basis are you maintaining that it's not an accurate reflection of the answer that the witness gave? If someone could explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I could if you like. I think the witness did say Mr. Deronjic, so it's not inaccurate. But I was going to clarify it, and I'll just ask was he referring to Mr. Deronjic or someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I asked to you describe, or I'm asking to you describe Mr. Beara a little bit, and in the record for some reason you started to describe a person and it was written or referenced Mr. Deronjic was, I think, somewhat taller, somewhat taller and had grey a hair as compared to Mr. Popovic. And just so the record is clear, who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. I had known Deronjic well, and there were two others with him, and one of them had grey hair. I was referring to one of the others and not to Deronjic. And they say that this other man was Mr. Beara. And I never really met Mr. Beara as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how much taller was Mr. Beara than Mr. Deronjic, do you remember? If at all?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: They are about the same height.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how much taller was Mr. Beara than the other gentleman that you claim was Mr. Popovic? You say he was somewhat taller. Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: He is a bigger man than Popovic. That's what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, do you remember how much taller if at all he was than Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if General Mladic ever came to the IKM during the period of July 5th through the 11th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Two or three times, but I didn't really keep records.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know that. But your memory is fairly decent or excellent. Can you share with me on what dates you claim Mr. -- or General Mladic was at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe after the 7th. His first visit may have been on the 7th because it was a holiday, a St. John's day, and General Zivanovic accompanied General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you testified earlier today that you had a brief conversation with Mr. Trisic at the IKM on or about July 11th, 1995. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Not on the 11th, that was on the 9th, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My apologies. I didn't have it written down. On the 9th, you had a brief conversation with Major Trisic, correct? And you called it quote "purely information, an informational conversation."

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a conversation in passing by. It was very brief. There were Major Trisic, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, reconcile this for me, if you don't mind. I have here the testimony of Mr. Trisic from the Blagojevic case, May 2004, and if we just turn quickly to page 9348, and let me read what Mr. Trisic says about this conversation that the two of you had. Line 15, counsel. They proceed to question him and the question begins as follows. "All right. While you were at Pribicevac, did you have much, did you have any contact with Bozo Momcilovic. I know you saw him but did you speak with him?" On line 18 the answer, did you see him or did you speak to him by Mr. Trisic is, "No, I didn't." Do you know that Mr. Trisic said that he didn't speak to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: It is not correct. You should ask him why he said that. Maybe he did not want to get me involved when he provided his testimony. Maybe he wanted to get as few people as possible. I don't know why he didn't mention me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And maybe he told the truth, correct, sir? It's also a possibility or you don't accept that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that he did not tell the truth, and I adhere to what I said on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's all I have, Your Honours. Oh, wait. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is to go next? Mr. Zivanovic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Momcilovic. I'm Zoran Zivanovic and I represent Vujadin Popovic in this case. First of all I would like to ask you this: You've told us that your father was killed on the 7th of January in Kravica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how old was your father when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether at the time he was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed at his home some ten metres away from the main entrance to his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: His house?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, his house. He didn't want to leave, and 72 days later we found his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing that I would like to clarify with you. You've told us here that there are no visible consequences of the shelling of Srebrenica dating from that period. You were talking about the period that you spent at the IKM, I suppose. You said there was no shelling at the time when you were there which means at the beginning of July up to the 11th of July. Is that the period of time that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because we've had an occasion to see a lot of damaged buildings in Srebrenica, and we suppose that this was a result of shelling. Could you please explain for us whether this damage originates from the time before May or April 1993 because Srebrenica became an enclave?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: A lot of damage was inflicted between March and April 1993, before the enclave was proclaimed, and some of the houses had been torched during an infighting of Muslims in Srebrenica. For example the school and some others were torched. This was done by the Muslims. There are also bullet traces, but I don't know when these were inflicted. I worked there and I'm familiar with Srebrenica. I know the town very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I was reading in your statement that you provided to the Defence team of Colonel Blagojevic, I could see that you mentioned Vujadin Popovic as a person that you saw at the IKM. However in that statement of yours, it doesn't say that you saw him on the same day or at the same time with Mr. Beara and Mr. Deronjic. I'm asking you this: Are you sure that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic was at the IKM at the same time when Colonel Beara and/or Mr. Deronjic were there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: The counsel didn't ask me anything to that effect, but I can say that they were together. I have already said it today but if it's important I can repeat. They were there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, in addition to these people whom you saw on that day, which other officers were at the IKM at the time when Lieutenant-Colonel arrived?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: General Krstic, Mr. Jevdjevic, the liaison officer, and Colonel Vukota.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic or some other officers, Beara, Deronjic, did they talk to these people?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: It was customary for everybody who arrived to report to General and then to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how much time Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic spent in the area?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know when they left. I didn't pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't observe them leaving?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I had my things to tend to. I don't know when they left and where they went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic stayed there on the 11th of July and his visit was in relation to the NATO bombing. If I understand you well, the whole group arrived between the first and the second NATO campaign?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I've told you I don't know exactly, but during that period of time they did arrive, I'm not sure about the exact hour when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you said that there were a couple of hours between the two campaigns?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You could not tell us about the time of the first and the second air strike?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. The first one came around 10.00 and the other one about 1.00 or 2.00 p.m. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Finally let me ask you this: You have told us that you probably saw Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic on television. Could you please tell me whether you remember in what situation did that happen, what was going on?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the circumstances of his appearance and I don't know when. It may have been even much later than 1995. I really wouldn't know. I know that I saw him, but I don't know the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't remember what kind of show it was and what was being said?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can't remember when you saw the programme?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't. I don't know exactly when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Momcilovic.

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm Jelena Nikolic and I represent Mr. Nikolic in this case. I would like to put some questions to you in relation to your testimony. You resided in Kravica before 1992 and after 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know Drago Nikolic's family from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We are from the same village. My first neighbour is his older brother, Dragan, and his house is some 100 metres away from my house. Currently this house is inhabited by his parents and his brother Dragan is in Bratunac. He resides in an apartment. He works in Bratunac. I know the entire family. I know his other brothers as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What about Drago Nikolic? Does he have any more brothers?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did have two. The younger one died, and the second eldest is my generation. We went to the same school. We played football on the same team. We see each other. I see him when he visits his father.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that you socialise, that you communicate, that you belong to the same generation, with one of the Nikolic brothers, would you be aware of the fact that in the Drago Nikolic's family there are members of other religions and ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Milan, one of his brothers, is married to a Catholic woman. They reside in Novi Sad. Very nice family. She is a very nice woman. His son is the same generation as my son. That's how we know each other well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In all this socialising, in all the communication that you had with them, did you ever communicate with Drago Nikolic, did you ever socialise with him?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: He is a bit older than me. Usually younger people know older people. I know that he attended a military school. I don't know much about him. I was much younger. Later on I went to school in Belgrade. He worked in Sarajevo. We didn't see each other that often. He would visit his father in Bacici and his brother Dragan was somewhat closer to me, but we did see each other, especially after 1996, because for a while he was in the immediate vicinity and we would see each other. We would even talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But you continued socialising with his brothers?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. With my neighbour Dragan, we continued socialising. He worked in Bratunac. I work in Srebrenica, and we see each other almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: With all this socialising and communication with them, did you ever hear any of them having any family problems? Did you ever hear of Drago Nikolic expressing any negative feelings towards his sister-in-law or other religions?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No, his father had four sons, three of whom graduated from university. They are very good family. A family held in high esteem. They keep together. I've never heard of any problems in the family.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In other words, Drago Nikolic never expressed any feelings of interethnic hatred?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No, he is a very nice person. I know his older brother and his younger brother better, but as far as I know, I've never heard any such thing about Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something about a tragedy that happened to you 1992. Your father was killed on that day, and my learned friends have already asked you about that. He was killed on Christmas 1993. What happened to other elderly and infirm people who remained in the village? You did tell us that some people remained?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: The 7th of January was the most tragic day in the history of my village, Kravica. Some 38 people were killed and some ten were wounded, the whole village was torched, a majority of the 38 were elderly people. For example, the Popovici, the Jokovici [phoen], Stanojevici [phoen] and other family members were all over 60, none of them remained alive. The only two people who were captured in Kravica were captured on the 8th or on the 9th and taken to Srebrenica. One of them testified here. His name was Ratko Nikolic, and after the time that he spent in prison he was slowly dying. He is my uncle. He weighs 50 kilos, not more today. And another woman who remained alive, I believe that she's also close to her death bed at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. Momcilovic, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Ms. Nikolic. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Momcilovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Miodrag Stojanovic and together with my colleagues I defend Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin. I would like to ask you to clarify some parts of the statement that you provided to Mr. Blagojevic's Defence. You mentioned that during your stay at the IKM, amongst others, you saw and you heard that members of the Special Police also came there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I know that this is what it says in the statement, but in my view, everybody who didn't belong to the Bratunac police was somebody else, if somebody different, I didn't know any of the men that did drop by the IKM post and that looked like members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What we are suggesting to you and to the Trial Chamber is that on the 11th, Ljubomir Borovcanin, together with at least two more members of the Republika Srpska MUP, who were not people from Bratunac, did arrive at the IKM with an intention to take orders from General Krstic on the use of the unit that were supposed to arrive in Bratunac around that time. My question to you would be this: Do you know Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin from 1992 when he arrived in our town as a refugee from Kladanj. At the time I was the general manager of the brick works. I met him. He spent sometime at the police station in Bratunac. And if he had been there, I would have recognised him. Once you meet a person like that you can't miss him. You can't not recognise him. So I'm sure that during the period of time while I was there, I did not see Mr. Borovcanin at that command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you agree that members of the MUP did arrive. You heard of them arriving?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There were people coming by, but if they were not in the Bratunac police, whom I knew, I wouldn't pay much attention, save for the Bratunac Brigade I didn't know anybody else. I didn't even know any other members of the army who did not belong to the Bratunac Brigade, and I really claim with certainty that Mr. Borovcanin was not there. I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And there is one more thing that I would like to ask you. According to the information that we have, at the general area of the Pribicevac IKM, there was the command trench or the command location which was a make makeshift shift tent where General Krstic would also spend the time, and even further away was an observation post from which the view of Srebrenica was much better?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would that description correspond the reality of the situation?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And one more question: When describing this place, we can also say that the communications or the signals centre was also there; i.e., there was a vehicle, a signals vehicle, that was the hub for the communications?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the vicinity of the command post, maybe a couple metres away or maybe ten metres away from the command post itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how far that place was from the observation point that you described for us?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: That communications centre was some 4 or five metres from the command post, and now you can calculate the distance yourself if you know how far the observation post was from the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And just let me complete this series of questions. Can we agree that the second NATO air strike was around 1400 or 1500 hours on that day, on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what I said and it happened in the sector closer to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that Ljubomir Borovcanin was in the area in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. On the assumption that the Miletic and Pandurevic teams still do not require to cross-examine the witness, I'm asking you whether you ever any redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have a very brief redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Momcilovic, you've mentioned a gentleman by the name of Jevdjevic in connection with his being a liaison officer. First, do you recall this gentleman's first name?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I know his last name, Jevdzevic. For me that was quite enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Second is, do you know what he did in relation to his responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just think it's outside the scope of the cross. He covered the area on direct with this witness, and now he's just following up questions that apparently he didn't ask him during his direct. But we are just formally saying that it's outside the scope and we should follow that procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. How does it link to the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think he -- several questions were put to him with respect to Mr. Jevdjevic, including the spelling of his name, who he was, what he did, on cross-examination. And I think this directly relates to that line of questioning. It was a very specific question which even involved the spelling of his name into the record. I can't recall which counsel put it to him, but I think it was Mr. Krgovic, and I'm simply trying to establish the identity of the person for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any doubt, any controversy, amongst you, as to who this Jevdjevic was? Can't this be stipulated rather than waste time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm perfectly willing to stipulate to it, and think we can do that, so I'll just move on to a different area, if I can accept that. [Prosecution counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, would you care to stipulate to Mr. Jevdjevic's identity for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you're -- yes, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he was not a liaison officer. He had a different assignment, if we talk about Milenko Jevdjevic. Perhaps I could discuss outside the courtroom with Mr. Vanderpuye. He was the commander of the communications battalion of the Drina Corps and that was his assignment, and his name is Milenko Jevdjevic, if we are referring to the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That justifies the Trial Chamber in deciding to give you the go ahead and proceed with your questions if the idea or the intention is to establish his identity. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think for the purposes of the record, Mr. Momcilovic, you've heard what Mr. Krgovic has said, is that an accurate -- is that accurate as to whom this Mr. Jevdjevic is that you've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was an officer from the corps. I didn't know exactly what his assignment was. But he did work in communications, and he had young or fresh soldiers under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have P00033, please, in e-court, shown to the witness? This is a communication, if we could just go down to the bottom, from General Tolimir, and it is addressed to, if we could just go to the top, it's addressed to Generals Gvero and Krstic at the IKM. I want to refer you specifically to paragraph number 2. If you could just read that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: What should I do with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would just ask you to read to yourself paragraph number 2, and if we could just page up to the top of the document, you can see that it's dated 09.07.1995 at the top left. That's the 9th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: This is in accordance with the statement that General Gvero on the 9th of July was there, and as he was with General Krstic. This communication was probably received through the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2 of this communication, there is an indication in that paragraph that the president has been satisfied with the combat operations thus far and is effectively given the go ahead for further combat operations, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No need for me to comment. It clearly says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I just want to be sure. Are you suggesting then that on the 9th of July that there was no combat operations that were proceeding in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: The phase of separating the enclaves had been completed by the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I have nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please allow me to ask a question about this document. I didn't want to interrupt. It refers to the stamp and the time at which it was received at the IKM. I would like to ask the witness a question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll up so that we see the stamp of receipt, the receipt stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Momcilovic, you can see the date the 9th of July and the time when this document was -- it's at 2350?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Much later than the general's visit at Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At the time this was received, General Gvero was no longer at Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No. We were -- we had already packed and moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Momcilovic, that brings your testimony to an end. We haven't got any further questions for you. Our staff will give you all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of my colleagues, Judge Kwon, Judge Prost, and Judge Stole, and on behalf of the Tribunal in general, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence and we all wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents or exhibits? Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have just the two, one being the map which is P02870, and the second being the document I've just used -- I'm sorry, the second is the map marked PIC 00140. And the -- that's correct, the last document is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Any of the Defence teams wishes to tender any documents? I don't think so. That closes that chapter. Let me come back to you now before we have the break and the next witness to what we were discussing very briefly yesterday in anticipation of the response from the Popovic Defence team relating to the motion for videolink. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next witness? There are no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Joseph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of a solemn declaration confirming that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth and the whole truth. Please go ahead, read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Joseph. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer for the Office of the Prosecutor will go first. He will then be followed by the various Defence teams on cross-examination. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We speak the same language. Nevertheless it needs to be translated, so I just ask you to keep a pause between my question and your answer, if you could, please. Sir, would you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Edward Paul Joseph.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I am 49 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how you're employed, what do you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I'm with Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, I'm an adjunct professor and visiting scholar.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is the subject matter of your teaching?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I am in the field of conflict management.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about your educational background, particularly as it relates to the former Yugoslavia, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I have a law degree from University of Virginia. I also have a bachelor and master's degree from Johns Hopkins university in international studies and from the same school where I teach the school of advanced international studies. Also I did military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while we're on that topic can you just describe what your military service was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I was an army aviator helicopter pilot, US army reserve. I also was on active duty in Bosnia for approximately almost one year in 199-- late 1995 and early 1996 until actually late fall 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is your level of proficiency with the B/C/S language as we refer to it here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I am reasonably proficient in that language now; although, I'm not formally trained and I'm not grammatically perfect in the language. But I'm reasonably proficient in that language.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you take a few moments and review for the Trial Chamber your employment history, again particularly as it relates to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I will be happy to do that. I was serving as a lawyer with the US arms control and disarmament agency. That's now formally part of the state department. Then it was quasi-independent. I was working in Geneva on arms control negotiations with the then Soviet Union and following that with Russian Federation. I was co-legal adviser for the start treaty when it was signed in 1991. In 1992, the summer, as an army reservist, I had to perform service, so I was ordered to assist UNHCR that was conducting an air lift to Sarajevo beginning in July 1992. It was during that time there were many difficulties on the ground, at the airport in Sarajevo, and so I volunteered to go down after completion of my military reserve service, and I was sent down by UNHCR to Sarajevo beginning in August and September 1992. I then was hired by UNPROFOR as a civilian, as a civil affairs officer, and worked with UNPROFOR as a civil affairs officer from October 1992 until late August 1995. And I was deployed in many, many locations in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you right there for a moment, if I could. Can you describe just generally what the duties and responsibilities of a civil affairs officer were and typically are?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Yes. I can. We performed a number of different functions, in a constantly evolving environment. We performed several different roles as political officers, as humanitarian officers, as diplomatic, and even legal to some degree and even at times related to media. So we were a all-points person for the UNPROFOR military chain to be in contact with and having direct line, say, from the UN political side, the UN, the formal UN headquarters in New York and the headquarters that were there in former Yugoslavia. So we had several different, a number of different roles, that were combined in many respects and depending on the situation were called upon to do many different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, you were serving in a civilian capacity as a civilian -- civil affairs officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: That is correct. For the most of my time in Bosnia during the war, I was there as a civilian. I did one short active duty assignment but for the most part I was there as a civilian, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would, again, just briefly touch on some of your assignments leading up to July of 1995, basically where were you based, and just briefly describe the nature of the work you were doing during those assignments?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I will. I arrived in Sarajevo in 1992 with UNHCR. I was the air lift liaison. I was there during that rather chaotic period, the most prominent event of which was the downing of an Italian plane carrying aid into Sarajevo not far from the Sarajevo airport. And then I was with UNPROFOR, I was first deployed to Knin. So obviously working closely with the Serb leadership there in Knin for the rest of 1992 and early 1993, there were some major military events in January 1993 following a Croatian movement there at Maslenica bridge. And then was sent to Kiseljak which was the headquarters, the new headquarters of the UNPROFOR operation command in Bosnia, and moving from Sarajevo to Kiseljak and I worked there until late summer 1993 and then went to Mostar where, because of the crisis there, fighting between Croats and Bosniaks there in Mostar. So I worked in that situation, and then was sent from there to Bihac and worked in that situation for over a year, which involved a complex conflict involving Serbs and Muslims and as well a conflict in -- internal conflict between Muslims in Bihac. Then I was in Zagreb for a short while in early 1995, and then was sent in July 1995 to Tuzla, following the events in Srebrenica, I was sent there, and then to Zepa and Sarajevo again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just interrupt you for a moment and take a quick detour and then we'll resume the balance of your employment history. During your work as a civil affairs officer, up to, say, June or July of 1995, did you have any contacts with senior VRS officers?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: In 1993, as -- when I was based in Kiseljak at UNPROFOR headquarters, yes, I had a contact with the senior Serb military leadership. At these meetings we would have negotiations at Sarajevo airport involving all three sides and UNPROFOR, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall the names of these high level senior VRS officers?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: There were a number. Of course, our most prominent was General Mladic. I recall General Tolimir and General Gvero as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many times approximately you met with these senior VRS officers?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: A number of times. There were a number of meetings at Sarajevo airport in 1993 and anywhere between a half a dozen and a dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That would be for each of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Right. At each -- generally, they were all present, not necessarily all three present at every meeting, but I had contact with them at various meetings during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We all know where General Mladic stood. But based on your contacts with generals Gvero and Tolimir, what was your understanding as to their place in this senior VRS hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: My understanding was that General Mladic was at the top and that in order General Tolimir and then General Gvero. That was my understanding as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you ever meet General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I don't recall meeting General Milovanovic, no, but I knew of him and had heard of him and had knew other UNPROFOR military who had met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you aware at the time of what General Milovanovic's position was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I was told he was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at the time did you know where that position fit in the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I wasn't exactly clear as to whether that meant definitively that he was of more a senior rank than the others. It wasn't precisely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I interrupted you, sir, in your employment history. You indicated that you were in Zepa in 1995, and I believe you've already told us you were in a different capacity in 1996. If you would pick it up there, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: As I said I was sent to Tuzla to work with our team there, civil affairs officer in Tuzla, who had responsibility for Srebrenica, and the -- what we were then anticipating was this wave of refugees from Srebrenica, and then was sent to Zepa following that, and then - I can give detail if that's required - and then in late August 1995 I returned to the United States, I worked during the fall of 1995 at the council on foreign relations in New York, and then was called to active duty with the army after the Dayton agreement was signed. And from late 1995 until late fall 1996 I was on active duty with the US army as part of the IFOR contingent. I was again with the civil affairs part, although, this time with the military and was assigned to OSCE at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you do with OSCE?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: With OSCE I was adviser to the head of mission and I worked on democratisations, so I was the director of the initial democratisation group in Sarajevo and I did that until late 1996. When I came off active duty, I was rehired by OSCE and was sent initially to Mostar, and I was the regional director in Mostar; that is, the senior OSCE official in Mostar for most of 1997. And then following some threats against me, I was removed by the head of mission and moved to Brcko where I also served for a year, all of 1998. I was the OSCE director in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And after that work?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: After that I assisted the Brcko arbitrator in the decision on Brcko and then in March, that decision was handed down in March 1999, shortly thereafter the air campaign started, the NATO air campaign in Kosovo, and I was hired by Catholic Relief Services to be the senior camp manager of a refugee camp on the border between Kosovo and Macedonia, that was a refugee camp for Kosovar-Albanian, primarily Albanian refugees from Kosovo during the air campaign, and then after that episode finished and Albanians returned to Kosovo, I went to Kosovo with CRS and worked in CRS until the end of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I returned to the United States, I worked on the presidential campaign of Al Gore, and following that unfortunate demise, I -- after the Florida debacle, I returned to the Balkans and I was hired by the United Nations and sent to Mitrovica municipality in Kosovo, which is as you probably know -- as the Court probably knows is another divided city, like Mostar, like Brcko, and I was the deputy municipal administrator in Brcko during that time obviously working with both Serbs and Albanians in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And approximately what year was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: That was late 2000 and for the first part of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And generally since then what kind of work have you been engaged in other than your teaching and studies?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: There was one other Balkans assignment. The conflict then started in Macedonia between Albanians and Macedonians that summer, and I was hired by the International Crisis Group and I was their projects director in Macedonia from August 2001 to August 2003 upon which time I returned to the United States and worked in think tanks and published articles on the Balkans, and I worked in Iraq as a civilian in fall 2004 and in Haiti in 2005 and 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, welcome to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to July of 1995, sir. You already spoke a little bit about this, but can you please tell the Trial Chamber how you first became involved in the events immediately following the fall of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Yes. I was sent -- I was asked by head of civil affairs at UNPROFOR in Zagreb to go immediately to Tuzla because there was the anticipation of thousands of refugees from Srebrenica, which had just fallen so that's what I did, and I was sent there to work with our civil affairs team there that was already in place at the Tuzla air base.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember the approximate date you I arrived in Tuzla, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: On or about 12 or 13 July 1995, on or about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what your experience was at that air base with the refugees as they were arriving?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Well, in one word, I will put it this way, we were overwhelmed. We were absolutely overwhelmed. I was there when the first buses arrived of these refugees, the vast, vast majority of whom were women if not all women, and we were quite overwhelmed in our ability to care and find adequate housing for them, obviously tent and so forth, at the air base, and to accommodate them and deal with their both emotional situation and their basic needs. There was some 20.000 plus in a little over 24 hours, and as I said, overwhelmed is the word that would describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to speak with any of these refugees during this time, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I did. I did speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from what you observed of them and from speaking with them, with these women, what kind of emotional and physical condition were they in when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I would say the best word to describe it is distraught. They were quite distraught. And their overwhelming source of distress was their concern about the fate of their men, be they husbands, fathers, sons or brothers, whom they had left behind, and that was very, very clear to me. In addition, there was obvious the chaos of accommodating so many people there and the inadequate means that we had at first to do it, but the -- that was the main source of the distress and that was quite apparent.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Are there any examples of this concern or distress that stand out in your mind, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Yes. I remember I have an image, a clear image, of one woman and I should say they were all reasonably thin, quite thin, was another sort of distinct memory that I have of them which was the case in many parts of Bosnia that -- where people were relatively deprived and isolated. And I have an image in my mind of a woman who had wandered away from the main part where we had grouped these refugees, and there was a barbed wire perimeter, because obviously these are military installations, and this woman was attempting to scale, with her bare hands, was attempting to scale the barbed wire fence and I asked her what she was doing and she was absolutely determined to scale because a rumour had circulated that the -- some men, some of the Srebrenica men, were nearby there, and she was determined that she was going to go explore and see if -- whether it was her son or husband was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall when you were there whether any of these buses that were arriving were escorted by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: No. I don't recall that there was an UNPROFOR escort with the bus. It's something that I recall. The first buses arrived at night, I recall, and there were other aspects of it that we were preoccupied with including questions of women who had gone missing from that so that was also what we were focused on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what were those questions, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: People claimed that some women had boarded and not gotten off at the other end, had been boarded in Srebrenica and not gotten off at the other end. That was a concern. There was also information that I had gotten that a woman was raped, and apparently this was again just information I heard, I didn't witness this, and I cannot confirm that it is true, that a woman had been raped and then hung herself at the Tuzla air base. I can't -- I did not witness that, however. But these were our preoccupations was working with UNHCR and others to try to establish the whereabouts and location and the well being of the these refugees amid what was a quite chaotic situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Approximately how long did you stay in Tuzla, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I believe it was about a week or so. Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I was then called to Sarajevo to the headquarters there in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: There was various debriefings and meetings that I was in, until events then shifted the focus to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber about that, sir, how did your focus become drawn to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Well, we became aware obviously we had UNPROFOR military assets on the ground in Zepa, and we became aware that the town was under attack and that there was a great deal of fighting and that there was a question of whether or not the town would fall or not, and then there was a flurry of meetings with senior officials in Bosnia and that became the next primary focus as to what would be the destiny of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you given a specific assignment, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Once the -- once -- at some point in time, there was a communication from General Mladic to General Smith, who was the BiH commander, and -- saying that he wanted UNPROFOR -- I believe specifying that he wanted UNPROFOR civil affairs, I don't know if it was that specific, but in an inviting some or in permitting some presence as we had no ability to go to -- into Republika Srpska without permission, and even sometimes with permission, we would have exceedingly great difficulty manoeuvring through Republika Srpska during the war, but there was this communication from General Mladic to General Smith saying to send some presence there and I and a colleague, Viktor Bezruchenko, were sent there to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall what the date was of your departure?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: It was on or about 20 July, somewhere around there, on or about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you just describe the trip that you had to take and tell the Trial Chamber, if you would, approximately when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Yes. We -- Viktor and I grabbed a map, we grabbed an up-armoured Land Rover and started on our way only to have a flat tire. I recall we had to return, get the tire fixed, and then continue on our way. And it took several hours because you had to go through a number of Serb check-points, a number, and we were -- we didn't believe we would ever make it because we had had "permission before," and had not made destination, as I said, it was extremely difficult to manoeuvre in Republika Srpska in those days, and so we were quite amazed to find ourselves later at the entrance point in the hill above Zepa later in that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe first of all, the -- do you recall whether this location had a particular name and can you describe it for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Right. The point that we arrived at was not in the centre of Zepa town. It was a point above it, Zepa lies in a gorge below. There is a river that flows through it and this very narrow steep heavily forested gorge, and at the top is a point that as I understood it was UNPROFOR military had given the name OP 2, observation point, observation post 2. And that is the point where we arrived. It was under control of Serb military forces. There were a lot of Serb army, what we called then BSA, Bosnian Serb army, I suppose today you say VRS but in those days we say BSA, the English initials, a lot of military. And we were told to wait, told quite firmly, "You will wait." And that's what we did until we had further instructions from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you just describe for a moment how the -- this OP 2 was physically set up? What did it consist in?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Again going from my memory now, it wasn't much. It was basically in a clearing, and there -- there were not really significant structures there. There might have been a perimeter fence and some meagre housing facility for the UNPROFOR troops who were there, may or may not have been there, or a tent even. I might even have just simply been a tent. But there were a number of vehicles and there was this perimeter and where all the vehicles were, there -- these -- were Serb military vehicles and there might even have been a tank, if I can recall. I can't be sure but there might well have been a tank. There were some loudspeakers set up around there. And that's what I can tell you. It was just basically a clearing out in a very rural area of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see we are about two minutes from the break. With your permission, Mr. President, I'm about to go into another area. I would ask that we take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Thank you, Mr. Joseph. We'll see you again tomorrow morning. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With your permission I would like to return to the question that you asked me earlier about the force of the subpoena to be issued for someone in the United States. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Joseph, I think, can leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to make my replies more precise. About the force of the subpoena. The international court in accordance with the chapter 7 of the Charter of the United Nations has some obligations for member countries; namely, the unconditional cooperation with the international court and to execute instructions for -- to provide assistance. This principle of compulsory cooperation between UN member states and the International Tribunal can be seen in Article 29 of the Statute. Paragraph 2 of that article says that the states must respond to all instructions given by the Trial Chamber. This provision includes some -- nothing new, but if we read that in the light of Articles 56 and 58 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Rule 58 says that the obligations contained in Article 59 of the Statute are above all legal obstacles that national systems or extradition agreements signed by the state in question could be against the transfer or extradition of the witness of the International Tribunal. Likewise, Article 56 of the -- says that the state that has been instructed to transfer the witness will, without delay, do everything that is necessary to effectively execute that instruction. Your Honours, that is public international law, that is applied in this Court. The only thing I would like to say with regard to this is that in the light of these provisions, we with all due respect, claim that it would be wrong to try to establish what could be done in the United States if the Trial Chamber issues a subpoena. That the Trial Chamber should limit itself only to such legal provisions pertaining to it, and then possibly decide on measures to be taken if somebody in the United States should oppose the measures taken by the Trial Chamber. I wanted to make this more precise so that you do not get the impression that I provided a too simplified answer to your question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. We are grateful for that elaboration. We are still discussing as you may have gathered otherwise we would have handed down the decision. We are still discussing, and we are hopeful that we should be in a position to hand down a decision tomorrow morning. So we stand adjourned. I thank the staff, the interpreters and operators, for having stayed with us a few more minutes. My apologies to the other Trial Chamber. Please do explain although I don't know if this will make a real difference. Thank you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
